title: Given two sorted arrays, find the median of the combined sorted order. Explain how the K-way Merge pattern locates the middle without fully merging, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Median of Two Sorted Arrays (K-way Merge View of the Middle Element)
keyPoints: This is a two-way merge (K=2) that stops at the middle position instead of merging everything.
For odd combined length, the median is the single middle value; for even, it is the average of the two middle values.
The merge-to-the-middle approach runs in O(M+N) linear time.
For monetary data, use BigDecimal to average the two middle values without precision loss.
A binary search solution exists that achieves O(log(min(M,N))) time but is more complex.
The merge view is the clean K-way Merge pattern answer for interviews.

s1_definition.oneliner: Two-way merge the sorted arrays but stop at the middle position to read off the median.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Median of Two Sorted Arrays** via K-way Merge advances a two-way merge to the middle position only.
- Keep indices into both arrays, repeatedly take the **smaller head**, and count consumed elements.
- For **odd** combined length, the median is the single middle value at position `n/2`.
- For **even** combined length, the median is the **average** of positions `n/2 - 1` and `n/2`.
- Time is **O(M + N)** linear; a binary search variant achieves **O(log(min(M, N)))** but is more complex.
- For money, average with `BigDecimal` to avoid precision loss.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has two sorted lists of customer account balances from two regional branches. To report the typical balance of the combined customer base, they need the median. A clerk walks both lists together, always taking the smaller next balance, counting steps, and stops at the middle. There is no need to write out the whole combined list.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Median of Two Sorted Arrays, framed through the K-way Merge pattern, is a two-way merge that you stop at the middle instead of running to completion. You keep an index into each array, repeatedly take the smaller of the two current heads, and count how many elements you have consumed. Because both arrays are already sorted, walking them together produces the combined order element by element, and you only need to reach the middle position.

For the combined length you decide the median rule up front. If the total is odd, the median is the single value at the middle consumed position. If the total is even, it is the average of the two middle values, so you remember both the previous and current values as you merge. For monetary data, you average using BigDecimal to avoid precision loss.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this to report a typical customer balance across two regional branches whose balance lists were each already sorted. He merged the two lists only as far as the middle and read off the median, averaging with BigDecimal when the combined count was even. The linear pass handled the large customer bases efficiently.

The senior-level insight is understanding that this is K-way Merge with K equal to 2, that you stop at the middle rather than merging everything, and that a binary search variant exists for O(log(min(M,N))) time. Being able to explain both approaches and when each is appropriate demonstrates range.

Remember one sentence: two-way merge to the middle position gives the median in linear time; binary search on the shorter array gives it in logarithmic time.
